translations.title: What Is Volume?
translations.explanation: What Is Volume? is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Finding Volume”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:5.MD.C.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Recognize volume as an attribute of solid figures and understand concepts of volume measurement. a. A cube with side length 1 unit, called a “unit cube,” is said to have “one cubic unit” of volume, and can be used to measure volume. b. A solid figure which can be packed without gaps or overlaps using n unit cubes is said to have a volume of n cubic units. Instructional focus: Students connect measurable attributes with units, measurement procedures, representations of data, and calculations that answer a concrete question. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: What Is Volume?. Choose a unit that matches the attribute, use equal-size units without gaps or overlaps, record the unit with the number, and interpret tables, line plots, clocks, money, area, volume, or angle measures according to the problem.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle measures 9 units by 4 units. Its area is 9 × 4 = 36 square units, while its perimeter is 2(9+4) = 26 units. Example 2: A rectangle measures 12 units by 3 units. Its area is 12 × 3 = 36 square units, while its perimeter is 2(12+3) = 30 units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify the requested attribute and units. Step 2: for area, multiply length by width: 9×4=36. Step 3: for perimeter, add all side lengths: 2(9+4)=26. Step 4: attach square units to area and linear units to perimeter. Step 1: identify the requested attribute and units. Step 2: for area, multiply length by width: 12×3=36. Step 3: for perimeter, add all side lengths: 2(12+3)=30. Step 4: attach square units to area and linear units to perimeter.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: What Is Volume?. A number without its unit can be incomplete. Do not mix incompatible units before converting them. In graphs, read the scale and labels before drawing conclusions; in geometric measurement, distinguish length, area, angle, and volume.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: What Is Volume?. Identify what is measured, choose or convert units correctly, calculate or read the representation, and state the result with its unit and meaning.

Krok 4: przy polu zapisz jednostki kwadratowe, a przy obwodzie liniowe. Krok 1: rozpoznaj mierzoną wielkość i jednostkę. Krok 2: pole: 12×3=36. Krok 3: obwód: 2(12+3)=30. translations.title: Use Layers to Determine Volume PLC Activity
translations.explanation: Use Layers to Determine Volume PLC Activity is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Finding Volume”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:5.MD.C.5, CCSS:5.OA.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Relate volume to the operations of multiplication and addition and solve real world and mathematical problems involving volume. a. Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with whole-number side lengths by packing it with unit cubes, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths, equivalently by multiplying the height by the area of the base. Represent threefold whole- number products as volumes, e.g., to repr esent the associative property of multiplication. b. Apply the formulas V = l × w × h and V = b × h for rectangular prisms to find volumes of right r ectangular prisms with whole-number edge lengths in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems. c. Recognize volume as additive. Find volumes of solid figures composed of two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms by adding the volumes of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real world problems. Write simple expressions that record calculations with numbers, and interpret numerical expressions without evaluating them. For example, express the calculation “add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2” as 2 × (8 + 7). Recognize that 3 × (18932 + 921) is three times as large as 18932 + 921, without having to calculate the indicated sum or product. Instructional focus: Students connect measurable attributes with units, measurement procedures, representations of data, and calculations that answer a concrete question. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.

translations.title: Expressions for Volume

Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with whole-number side lengths by packing it with unit cubes, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths, equivalently by multiplying the height by the area of the base. Represent threefold whole- number products as volumes, e.g., to repr esent the associative property of multiplication. b. Apply the formulas V = l × w × h and V = b × h for rectangular prisms to find volumes of right r ectangular prisms with whole-number edge lengths in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems. c. Recognize volume as additive. Find volumes of solid figures composed of two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms by adding the volumes of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real world problems. Use parentheses, brackets, or braces in numerical expressions, and evaluate expressions with these symbols. Write simple expressions that record calculations with numbers, and interpret numerical expressions without evaluating them. For example, express the calculation “add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2” as 2 × (8 + 7). Recognize that 3 × (18932 + 921) is three times as large as 18932 + 921, without having to calculate the indicated sum or product. Instructional focus: Students reason about equal groups, arrays, factors, products, quotients, and unknown group sizes. Multiplication and division are connected inverse relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Expressions for Volume. A product can represent equal groups or rows and columns. Division can ask how many groups or how many objects are in each group. Factor pairs describe the same product, and multiplication can be checked with division.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Arrange 3 equal groups with 2 objects in each group. The product is 3 × 2 = 6; therefore 6 ÷ 3 = 2. Example 2: Arrange 6 equal groups with 2 objects in each group. The product is 6 × 2 = 12; therefore 12 ÷ 6 = 2.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify 3 groups and 2 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 3 by 2 to get 6. Step 3: interpret 6 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 6 ÷ 3 = 2. Step 1: identify 6 groups and 2 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 6 by 2 to get 12. Step 3: interpret 12 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 12 ÷ 6 = 2.

translations.explanation: All Kinds of Prisms is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Finding Volume”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:5.MD.C.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Relate volume to the operations of multiplication and addition and solve real world and mathematical problems involving volume. a. Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with whole-number side lengths by packing it with unit cubes, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths, equivalently by multiplying the height by the area of the base. Represent threefold whole- number products as volumes, e.g., to repr esent the associative property of multiplication. b. Apply the formulas V = l × w × h and V = b × h for rectangular prisms to find volumes of right r ectangular prisms with whole-number edge lengths in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems. c. Recognize volume as additive. Find volumes of solid figures composed of two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms by adding the volumes of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real world problems. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: All Kinds of Prisms. translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle measures 4 units by 6 units. Its area is 4 × 6 = 24 square units, while its perimeter is 2(4+6) = 20 units. Example 2: A rectangle measures 10 units by 3 units. Its area is 10 × 3 = 30 square units, while its perimeter is 2(10+3) = 26 units.

Step 3: for perimeter, add all side lengths: 2(10+3)=26. Step 4: attach square units to area and linear units to perimeter.

translations.title: Share Sandwiches
translations.explanation: Share Sandwiches is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Fractions as Quotients and Fraction Multiplication”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:5.NF.B.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Interpret a fraction as division of the numerator by the denominator (a/b = a ÷ b). Solve word problems involving division of whole numbers leading to answers in the form of fractions or mixed numbers, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem. For example, interpret 3/4 as the result of dividing 3 by 4, noting that 3/4 multiplied by 4 equals 3, and that when 3 wholes are shared equally among 4 people each person has a share of size 3/4. If 9 people want to share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight, how many pounds of rice should each person get? Between what two whole numbers does your answer lie? Instructional focus: Students interpret fractions as numbers and as relationships between equal parts and a whole, then use equivalent forms and operations only when their meaning is preserved. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Share Sandwiches. The denominator tells how many equal parts make one whole; the numerator counts those parts. Equivalent fractions name the same point or quantity. For addition and subtraction, units must be the same size; for multiplication or division, interpret what is being scaled or shared.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Add fractions with the same unit: 4/9 + 4/9 = 8/9. This equals 8/9 in simplest form. Example 2: Add fractions with the same unit: 4/6 + 4/6 = 8/6. This equals 4/3 in simplest form.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: both fractions count 9ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 4+4=8. Step 3: keep denominator 9. Step 4: simplify 8/9 to 8/9 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness. Step 1: both fractions count 6ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 4+4=8. Step 3: keep denominator 6. Step 4: simplify 8/6 to 4/3 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Share Sandwiches. Do not add denominators when adding fractions. Do not cancel terms across addition. Always ask whether the fraction is less than, equal to, or greater than one when estimating the reasonableness of an answer.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Share Sandwiches. Identify the fractional unit, preserve equal-sized parts, use equivalence when needed, perform the operation, and check the size of the answer.

translations.title: Ułamki — Share Sandwiches
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Ułamki — Share Sandwiches” należy do działu „Fractions as Quotients and Fraction Multiplication” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:5.NF.B.3. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń interpretuje ułamki jako liczby oraz jako relację równych części do całości, a następnie stosuje ułamki równoważne i działania wtedy, gdy zachowane jest ich znaczenie. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Ułamki — Share Sandwiches. Mianownik mówi, na ile równych części podzielono całość, a licznik wskazuje liczbę takich części. Ułamki równoważne opisują tę samą liczbę. Przy dodawaniu i odejmowaniu części muszą mieć ten sam rozmiar; przy mnożeniu i dzieleniu trzeba interpretować skalowanie lub podział.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Dodaj ułamki o tej samej jednostce: 4/9 + 4/9 = 8/9. Po skróceniu otrzymujemy 8/9. Przykład 2: Dodaj ułamki o tej samej jednostce: 4/6 + 4/6 = 8/6. Po skróceniu otrzymujemy 4/3.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: oba ułamki opisują części 1/9, więc jednostka jest wspólna. Krok 2: dodaj liczniki: 4+4=8. Krok 3: zachowaj mianownik 9. Krok 4: skróć 8/9 do 8/9 i porównaj wynik z 1. Krok 1: oba ułamki opisują części 1/6, więc jednostka jest wspólna. Krok 2: dodaj liczniki: 4+4=8. Krok 3: zachowaj mianownik 6. Krok 4: skróć 8/6 do 4/3 i porównaj wynik z 1.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Ułamki — Share Sandwiches. Nie dodawaj mianowników podczas dodawania ułamków i nie skracaj składników przez znak dodawania. Przy szacowaniu sprawdzaj, czy ułamek jest mniejszy, równy czy większy od jedności.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Ułamki — Share Sandwiches. Rozpoznaj jednostkę ułamkową, zachowaj równe części, w razie potrzeby użyj ułamków równoważnych, wykonaj działanie i sprawdź wielkość wyniku.

translations.title: Partial Products in Algorithms
translations.explanation: Partial Products in Algorithms is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Wrapping Up Multiplication and Division with Multi-Digit Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:5.OA.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Write simple expressions that record calculations with numbers, and interpret numerical expressions without evaluating them. For example, express the calculation “add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2” as 2 × (8 + 7). Recognize that 3 × (18932 + 921) is three times as large as 18932 + 921, without having to calculate the indicated sum or product. Instructional focus: Students reason about equal groups, arrays, factors, products, quotients, and unknown group sizes. Multiplication and division are connected inverse relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Partial Products in Algorithms. A product can represent equal groups or rows and columns. Division can ask how many groups or how many objects are in each group. Factor pairs describe the same product, and multiplication can be checked with division.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Arrange 8 equal groups with 5 objects in each group. The product is 8 × 5 = 40; therefore 40 ÷ 8 = 5. Example 2: Arrange 9 equal groups with 3 objects in each group. The product is 9 × 3 = 27; therefore 27 ÷ 9 = 3.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify 8 groups and 5 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 8 by 5 to get 40. Step 3: interpret 40 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 40 ÷ 8 = 5. Step 1: identify 9 groups and 3 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 9 by 3 to get 27. Step 3: interpret 27 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 27 ÷ 9 = 3.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Partial Products in Algorithms. Do not swap the meaning of number of groups and size of each group without checking the context. A remainder must be interpreted, not ignored automatically. Verify division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor when appropriate.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Partial Products in Algorithms. Model equal groups clearly, connect multiplication with division, compute accurately, and interpret the answer in context.

translations.title: Standard Algorithm: One-digit and Multi-digit Numbers with Composing
translations.explanation: Standard Algorithm: One-digit and Multi-digit Numbers with Composing is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Wrapping Up Multiplication and Division with Multi-Digit Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:5.NBT.B.5. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm. translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Standard Algorithm: One-digit and Multi-digit Numbers with Composing. A digit has a value determined by its position. Moving one place left multiplies place value by 10; moving one place right divides it by 10. Reliable algorithms preserve place value by aligning like units and regrouping only when needed.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The number 657 has 6 hundreds, 5 tens, and 7 ones, so 657 = 600 + 50 + 7. Adding 49 gives 657 + 49 = 706. Example 2: The number 268 has 2 hundreds, 6 tens, and 8 ones, so 268 = 200 + 60 + 8. Adding 61 gives 268 + 61 = 329.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: decompose 657 by place value. Step 2: decompose 49 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Recognize volume as an attribute of solid figures and understand concepts of volume measurement. a. A cube with side length 1 unit, called a “unit cube,” is said to have “one cubic unit” of volume, and can be used to measure volume. b. A solid figure which can be packed without gaps or overlaps using n unit cubes is said to have a volume of n cubic units. Relate volume to the operations of multiplication and addition and solve real world and mathematical problems involving volume. a. Find the volume of a right rectangular prism with whole-number side lengths by packing it with unit cubes, and show that the volume is the same as would be found by multiplying the edge lengths, equivalently by multiplying the height by the area of the base. Represent threefold whole- number products as volumes, e.g., to repr esent the associative property of multiplication. b. Apply the formulas V = l × w × h and V = b × h for rectangular prisms to find volumes of right r ectangular prisms with whole-number edge lengths in the context of solving real world and mathematical problems. c. Recognize volume as additive. Find volumes of solid figures composed of two non-overlapping right rectangular prisms by adding the volumes of the non-overlapping parts, applying this technique to solve real world problems. Fluently multiply multi-digit whole numbers using the standard algorithm. Instructional focus: Students connect measurable attributes with units, measurement procedures, representations of data, and calculations that answer a concrete question. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.

translations.title: Different Partial Quotients PLC Activity
translations.explanation: Different Partial Quotients PLC Activity is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Wrapping Up Multiplication and Division with Multi-Digit Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:5.NBT.B.6, CCSS:5.OA.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Find whole-number quotients of whole numbers with up to four-digit dividends and two-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models. Write simple expressions that record calculations with numbers, and interpret numerical expressions without evaluating them. For example, express the calculation “add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2” as 2 × (8 + 7). Recognize that 3 × (18932 + 921) is three times as large as 18932 + 921, without having to calculate the indicated sum or product. Instructional focus: Students use the base-ten structure to read, compose, decompose, compare, round, and calculate with whole numbers or decimals at the grade-appropriate level. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Different Partial Quotients PLC Activity. A digit has a value determined by its position. Moving one place left multiplies place value by 10; moving one place right divides it by 10. Reliable algorithms preserve place value by aligning like units and regrouping only when needed.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The number 526 has 5 hundreds, 2 tens, and 6 ones, so 526 = 500 + 20 + 6. Adding 47 gives 526 + 47 = 573. Example 2: The number 275 has 2 hundreds, 7 tens, and 5 ones, so 275 = 200 + 70 + 5. Adding 39 gives 275 + 39 = 314.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: decompose 526 by place value. Step 2: decompose 47 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 573; estimate 526+about 47 to confirm the magnitude. Step 1: decompose 275 by place value. Step 2: decompose 39 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 314; estimate 275+about 39 to confirm the magnitude.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Different Partial Quotients PLC Activity. Do not compare numbers by looking at only one digit. Keep place values aligned in written calculations, especially with decimals. Estimate before or after computing so that misplaced digits and unreasonable answers are detected.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Different Partial Quotients PLC Activity. Use place value to represent the number, select an efficient operation or comparison strategy, and verify the magnitude of the result.

translations.explanation: Fractions as Partial Quotients (optional) is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Wrapping Up Multiplication and Division with Multi-Digit Numbers”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:5.OA.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Write simple expressions that record calculations with numbers, and interpret numerical expressions without evaluating them. For example, express the calculation “add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2” as 2 × (8 + 7). Recognize that 3 × (18932 + 921) is three times as large as 18932 + 921, without having to calculate the indicated sum or product. Instructional focus: Students reason about equal groups, arrays, factors, products, quotients, and unknown group sizes. Multiplication and division are connected inverse relationships. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Fractions as Partial Quotients (optional). A product can represent equal groups or rows and columns. Division can ask how many groups or how many objects are in each group. Factor pairs describe the same product, and multiplication can be checked with division.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Arrange 7 equal groups with 3 objects in each group. The product is 7 × 3 = 21; therefore 21 ÷ 7 = 3. Example 2: Arrange 8 equal groups with 5 objects in each group. The product is 8 × 5 = 40; therefore 40 ÷ 8 = 5.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify 7 groups and 3 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 7 by 3 to get 21. Step 3: interpret 21 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 21 ÷ 7 = 3. Step 1: identify 8 groups and 5 objects per group. Step 2: multiply 8 by 5 to get 40. Step 3: interpret 40 as the total. Step 4: check with the inverse relationship 40 ÷ 8 = 5.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Fractions as Partial Quotients (optional). Do not swap the meaning of number of groups and size of each group without checking the context. A remainder must be interpreted, not ignored automatically. Verify division by multiplying the quotient by the divisor when appropriate.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Fractions as Partial Quotients (optional). Model equal groups clearly, connect multiplication with division, compute accurately, and interpret the answer in context.

Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń wykorzystuje strukturę systemu dziesiętnego do odczytywania, składania, rozkładania, porównywania, zaokrąglania i wykonywania działań na liczbach całkowitych lub dziesiętnych odpowiednio do poziomu. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Wartość pozycyjna i działania w systemie dziesiętnym — Thousandths in Expanded Form. Wartość cyfry zależy od jej pozycji. Przesunięcie o jedno miejsce w lewo mnoży wartość pozycyjną przez 10, a w prawo dzieli ją przez 10. Poprawne algorytmy zachowują wartości pozycyjne przez ustawianie tych samych rzędów pod sobą i właściwe przegrupowanie.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Liczba 849 ma 8 setek, 4 dziesiątek i 9 jedności, więc 849 = 800 + 40 + 9. Po dodaniu 58 otrzymujemy 849 + 58 = 907. Przykład 2: Liczba 378 ma 3 setek, 7 dziesiątek i 8 jedności, więc 378 = 300 + 70 + 8. Po dodaniu 29 otrzymujemy 378 + 29 = 407.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: rozłóż 849 według wartości pozycyjnych. Krok 2: w razie potrzeby rozłóż 58. Krok 3: połącz te same rzędy i przegrupuj dziesięć jednostek w jednostkę wyższego rzędu. Krok 4: wynik to 907; oszacuj, aby sprawdzić jego wielkość. Krok 1: rozłóż 378 według wartości pozycyjnych. translations.title: Explore Place Value Relationships (optional)
translations.explanation: Explore Place Value Relationships (optional) is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Place Value Patterns and Decimal Operations”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:5.NBT.A.1, CCSS:5.NBT.A.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Recognize that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as it represents in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left. Read, write, and compare decimals to thousandths. a. Read and write decimals to thousandths using base-ten numerals, number names, and expanded form, e.g., 347.392 = 3 × 100 + 4 × 10 + 7 × 1 + 3 × (1/10) + 9 × (1/100) + 2 × (1/1000). b. Compare two decimals to thousandths based on meanings of the digits in each place, using >, =, and < symbols to record the results of comparisons. Instructional focus: Students use the base-ten structure to read, compose, decompose, compare, round, and calculate with whole numbers or decimals at the grade-appropriate level. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Explore Place Value Relationships (optional). A digit has a value determined by its position. Moving one place left multiplies place value by 10; moving one place right divides it by 10. Reliable algorithms preserve place value by aligning like units and regrouping only when needed.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The number 448 has 4 hundreds, 4 tens, and 8 ones, so 448 = 400 + 40 + 8. Adding 65 gives 448 + 65 = 513. Example 2: The number 574 has 5 hundreds, 7 tens, and 4 ones, so 574 = 500 + 70 + 4. Adding 67 gives 574 + 67 = 641.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: decompose 448 by place value. Step 2: decompose 65 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 513; estimate 448+about 65 to confirm the magnitude. Step 1: decompose 574 by place value. Step 2: decompose 67 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 641; estimate 574+about 67 to confirm the magnitude.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Explore Place Value Relationships (optional). Do not compare numbers by looking at only one digit. Keep place values aligned in written calculations, especially with decimals. Estimate before or after computing so that misplaced digits and unreasonable answers are detected.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Explore Place Value Relationships (optional). Use place value to represent the number, select an efficient operation or comparison strategy, and verify the magnitude of the result.

translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Multi-step Conversion Problems: Metric Liquid Volume. A digit has a value determined by its position. Moving one place left multiplies place value by 10; moving one place right divides it by 10. Reliable algorithms preserve place value by aligning like units and regrouping only when needed.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The number 295 has 2 hundreds, 9 tens, and 5 ones, so 295 = 200 + 90 + 5. Adding 62 gives 295 + 62 = 357. Example 2: The number 398 has 3 hundreds, 9 tens, and 8 ones, so 398 = 300 + 90 + 8. Adding 25 gives 398 + 25 = 423.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: decompose 295 by place value. Step 2: decompose 62 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 357; estimate 295+about 62 to confirm the magnitude. Step 1: decompose 398 by place value. Step 2: decompose 25 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 423; estimate 398+about 25 to confirm the magnitude.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Multi-step Conversion Problems: Metric Liquid Volume. Do not compare numbers by looking at only one digit. Keep place values aligned in written calculations, especially with decimals. Estimate before or after computing so that misplaced digits and unreasonable answers are detected.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Multi-step Conversion Problems: Metric Liquid Volume. Use place value to represent the number, select an efficient operation or comparison strategy, and verify the magnitude of the result.

The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions in such a way as to produce an equivalent sum or difference of fractions with like denominators. For example, 2/3 + 5/4 = 8/12 + 15/12 = 23/12. (In general, a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/bd.) Instructional focus: Students interpret fractions as numbers and as relationships between equal parts and a whole, then use equivalent forms and operations only when their meaning is preserved. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Add and Subtract Fractions PLC Activity. The denominator tells how many equal parts make one whole; the numerator counts those parts. Equivalent fractions name the same point or quantity. For addition and subtraction, units must be the same size; for multiplication or division, interpret what is being scaled or shared.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Add fractions with the same unit: 5/6 + 3/6 = 8/6. This equals 4/3 in simplest form. Example 2: Add fractions with the same unit: 3/7 + 1/7 = 4/7. This equals 4/7 in simplest form.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: both fractions count 6ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 5+3=8. Step 3: keep denominator 6. Step 4: simplify 8/6 to 4/3 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness. Step 1: both fractions count 7ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 3+1=4. Step 3: keep denominator 7. Step 4: simplify 4/7 to 4/7 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Add and Subtract Fractions PLC Activity. Do not add denominators when adding fractions. Do not cancel terms across addition. Always ask whether the fraction is less than, equal to, or greater than one when estimating the reasonableness of an answer.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Add and Subtract Fractions PLC Activity. Identify the fractional unit, preserve equal-sized parts, use equivalence when needed, perform the operation, and check the size of the answer.

translations.title: Add and Subtract Ułamki PLC Activity
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Add and Subtract Ułamki PLC Activity” należy do działu „More Decimal and Fraction Operations” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:5.NF.A.1. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń interpretuje ułamki jako liczby oraz jako relację równych części do całości, a następnie stosuje ułamki równoważne i działania wtedy, gdy zachowane jest ich znaczenie. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Add and Subtract Ułamki PLC Activity. Mianownik mówi, na ile równych części podzielono całość, a licznik wskazuje liczbę takich części. translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Dodaj ułamki o tej samej jednostce: 5/6 + 3/6 = 8/6. Po skróceniu otrzymujemy 4/3. Przykład 2: Dodaj ułamki o tej samej jednostce: 3/7 + 1/7 = 4/7. Po skróceniu otrzymujemy 4/7.

Krok 4: skróć 8/6 do 4/3 i porównaj wynik z 1. Krok 1: oba ułamki opisują części 1/7, więc jednostka jest wspólna. Krok 2: dodaj liczniki: 3+1=4. Krok 3: zachowaj mianownik 7. translations.title: Use Equivalent Expressions
translations.explanation: Use Equivalent Expressions is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “More Decimal and Fraction Operations”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:5.NF.A.1, CCSS:5.NF.A.2. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions in such a way as to produce an equivalent sum or difference of fractions with like denominators. For example, 2/3 + 5/4 = 8/12 + 15/12 = 23/12. (In general, a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/bd.) Solve word problems involving addition and subtraction of fractions referring to the same whole, including cases of unlike denominators, e.g., by using visual fraction models or equations to represent the problem. Use benchmark fractions and number sense of fractions to estimate mentally and assess the reasonableness of answers. For example, recognize an incorrect result 2/5 + 1/2 = 3/7, by observing that 3/7 < 1/2. Instructional focus: Students interpret fractions as numbers and as relationships between equal parts and a whole, then use equivalent forms and operations only when their meaning is preserved. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.

translations.title: Representing Fractions on a Line Plot

The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Use a pair of perpendicular number lines, called axes, to define a coordinate system, with the intersection of the lines (the origin) arranged to coincide with Instructional focus: Students describe, compose, decompose, compare, and reason about shapes using defining properties rather than appearance alone. translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Explore the Coordinate Grid. Geometric claims should use properties such as sides, angles, parallel or perpendicular lines, symmetry, coordinates, congruence, similarity, or equal partitions as appropriate. translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle with side lengths 3 and 2 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 3 × 2 = 6 square units. translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 3 and 2. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 6. translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Explore the Coordinate Grid. Name the relevant properties, represent the figure accurately, reason from those properties, and verify that the conclusion remains true when the picture changes orientation or scale.

translations.title: Dive Back Into Division
translations.explanation: Dive Back Into Division is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:5.G.B.3, CCSS:5.G.B.4, CCSS:5.NBT.B.6. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Understand that attributes belonging to a category of two-dimensional figures also belong to all subcategories of that category. For example, all rectangles have four right angles and squares are rectangles, so all squares have four right angles. Classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on properties. Find whole-number quotients of whole numbers with up to four-digit dividends and two-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models. Instructional focus: Students describe, compose, decompose, compare, and reason about shapes using defining properties rather than appearance alone. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Dive Back Into Division. Geometric claims should use properties such as sides, angles, parallel or perpendicular lines, symmetry, coordinates, congruence, similarity, or equal partitions as appropriate. A drawing is evidence only when its marked or known properties justify the conclusion.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle with side lengths 8 and 7 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 8 × 7 = 56 square units. Example 2: A rectangle with side lengths 8 and 5 has four right angles and opposite sides of equal length. Its area is 8 × 5 = 40 square units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 8 and 7. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 56. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties. Step 1: identify defining properties: four sides and four right angles. Step 2: use the given side lengths 8 and 5. Step 3: multiply to obtain area 40. Step 4: note that rotating the rectangle would not change its defining properties.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Dive Back Into Division. Do not classify a shape by orientation, color, or size when those are not defining attributes. Do not assume an angle or length from appearance; use the stated properties or calculate them.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Dive Back Into Division. Name the relevant properties, represent the figure accurately, reason from those properties, and verify that the conclusion remains true when the picture changes orientation or scale.

translations.title: Here Comes the Sum
translations.explanation: Here Comes the Sum is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:5.NF.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions in such a way as to produce an equivalent sum or difference of fractions with like denominators. For example, 2/3 + 5/4 = 8/12 + 15/12 = 23/12. (In general, a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/bd.) Instructional focus: Students interpret fractions as numbers and as relationships between equal parts and a whole, then use equivalent forms and operations only when their meaning is preserved. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Here Comes the Sum. The denominator tells how many equal parts make one whole; the numerator counts those parts. Equivalent fractions name the same point or quantity. For addition and subtraction, units must be the same size; for multiplication or division, interpret what is being scaled or shared.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Add fractions with the same unit: 6/8 + 6/8 = 12/8. This equals 3/2 in simplest form. Example 2: Add fractions with the same unit: 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8. This equals 5/8 in simplest form.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: both fractions count 8ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 6+6=12. Step 3: keep denominator 8. Step 4: simplify 12/8 to 3/2 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness. Step 1: both fractions count 8ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 2+3=5. Step 3: keep denominator 8. Step 4: simplify 5/8 to 5/8 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Here Comes the Sum. Do not add denominators when adding fractions. Do not cancel terms across addition. Always ask whether the fraction is less than, equal to, or greater than one when estimating the reasonableness of an answer.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Here Comes the Sum. Identify the fractional unit, preserve equal-sized parts, use equivalence when needed, perform the operation, and check the size of the answer.

Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń interpretuje ułamki jako liczby oraz jako relację równych części do całości, a następnie stosuje ułamki równoważne i działania wtedy, gdy zachowane jest ich znaczenie. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Ułamki — Here Comes the Sum. Mianownik mówi, na ile równych części podzielono całość, a licznik wskazuje liczbę takich części. Ułamki równoważne opisują tę samą liczbę. Przy dodawaniu i odejmowaniu części muszą mieć ten sam rozmiar; przy mnożeniu i dzieleniu trzeba interpretować skalowanie lub podział.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Dodaj ułamki o tej samej jednostce: 6/8 + 6/8 = 12/8. Po skróceniu otrzymujemy 3/2. Przykład 2: Dodaj ułamki o tej samej jednostce: 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8. Po skróceniu otrzymujemy 5/8.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: oba ułamki opisują części 1/8, więc jednostka jest wspólna. Krok 2: dodaj liczniki: 6+6=12. Krok 3: zachowaj mianownik 8. Krok 4: skróć 12/8 do 3/2 i porównaj wynik z 1. Krok 1: oba ułamki opisują części 1/8, więc jednostka jest wspólna. Krok 2: dodaj liczniki: 2+3=5. Krok 3: zachowaj mianownik 8. Krok 4: skróć 5/8 do 5/8 i porównaj wynik z 1.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Ułamki — Here Comes the Sum. Nie dodawaj mianowników podczas dodawania ułamków i nie skracaj składników przez znak dodawania. Przy szacowaniu sprawdzaj, czy ułamek jest mniejszy, równy czy większy od jedności.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Ułamki — Here Comes the Sum. Rozpoznaj jednostkę ułamkową, zachowaj równe części, w razie potrzeby użyj ułamków równoważnych, wykonaj działanie i sprawdź wielkość wyniku.

translations.title: What’s the Difference?
translations.explanation: What’s the Difference? is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:5.NF.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions in such a way as to produce an equivalent sum or difference of fractions with like denominators. For example, 2/3 + 5/4 = 8/12 + 15/12 = 23/12. (In general, a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/bd.) Instructional focus: Students interpret fractions as numbers and as relationships between equal parts and a whole, then use equivalent forms and operations only when their meaning is preserved. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: What’s the Difference?. The denominator tells how many equal parts make one whole; the numerator counts those parts. Equivalent fractions name the same point or quantity. For addition and subtraction, units must be the same size; for multiplication or division, interpret what is being scaled or shared.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Add fractions with the same unit: 2/6 + 2/6 = 4/6. This equals 2/3 in simplest form. Example 2: Add fractions with the same unit: 3/6 + 4/6 = 7/6. This equals 7/6 in simplest form.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: both fractions count 6ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 2+2=4. Step 3: keep denominator 6. Step 4: simplify 4/6 to 2/3 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness. Step 1: both fractions count 6ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 3+4=7. Step 3: keep denominator 6. Step 4: simplify 7/6 to 7/6 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: What’s the Difference?. Do not add denominators when adding fractions. Do not cancel terms across addition. Always ask whether the fraction is less than, equal to, or greater than one when estimating the reasonableness of an answer.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: What’s the Difference?. Identify the fractional unit, preserve equal-sized parts, use equivalence when needed, perform the operation, and check the size of the answer.

translations.title: Decimal Game Day
translations.explanation: Decimal Game Day is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:5.NBT.B.7. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Add, subtract, multiply, and divide decimals to hundredths, using concrete models or drawings and strategies based on place value, properties of operations, and/or the relationship between addition and subtraction; relate the strategy to a written method and explain the reasoning used. Instructional focus: Students use the base-ten structure to read, compose, decompose, compare, round, and calculate with whole numbers or decimals at the grade-appropriate level. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Decimal Game Day. A digit has a value determined by its position. Moving one place left multiplies place value by 10; moving one place right divides it by 10. Reliable algorithms preserve place value by aligning like units and regrouping only when needed.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The number 791 has 7 hundreds, 9 tens, and 1 ones, so 791 = 700 + 90 + 1. Adding 22 gives 791 + 22 = 813. Example 2: The number 753 has 7 hundreds, 5 tens, and 3 ones, so 753 = 700 + 50 + 3. Adding 39 gives 753 + 39 = 792.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: decompose 791 by place value. Step 2: decompose 22 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 813; estimate 791+about 22 to confirm the magnitude. Step 1: decompose 753 by place value. Step 2: decompose 39 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 792; estimate 753+about 39 to confirm the magnitude.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Decimal Game Day. Do not compare numbers by looking at only one digit. Keep place values aligned in written calculations, especially with decimals. Estimate before or after computing so that misplaced digits and unreasonable answers are detected.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Decimal Game Day. Use place value to represent the number, select an efficient operation or comparison strategy, and verify the magnitude of the result.

translations.title: Number Talk PLC Activity
translations.explanation: Number Talk PLC Activity is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:5.NBT.B.6. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Find whole-number quotients of whole numbers with up to four-digit dividends and two-digit divisors, using strategies based on place value, the properties of operations, and/or the relationship between multiplication and division. Illustrate and explain the calculation by using equations, rectangular arrays, and/or area models. Instructional focus: Students use the base-ten structure to read, compose, decompose, compare, round, and calculate with whole numbers or decimals at the grade-appropriate level. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Number Talk PLC Activity. A digit has a value determined by its position. Moving one place left multiplies place value by 10; moving one place right divides it by 10. Reliable algorithms preserve place value by aligning like units and regrouping only when needed.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: The number 616 has 6 hundreds, 1 tens, and 6 ones, so 616 = 600 + 10 + 6. Adding 37 gives 616 + 37 = 653. Example 2: The number 857 has 8 hundreds, 5 tens, and 7 ones, so 857 = 800 + 50 + 7. Adding 56 gives 857 + 56 = 913.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: decompose 616 by place value. Step 2: decompose 37 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 653; estimate 616+about 37 to confirm the magnitude. Step 1: decompose 857 by place value. Step 2: decompose 56 if helpful. Step 3: combine like place-value units and regroup when ten of a unit are formed. Step 4: the sum is 913; estimate 857+about 56 to confirm the magnitude.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Number Talk PLC Activity. Do not compare numbers by looking at only one digit. Keep place values aligned in written calculations, especially with decimals. Estimate before or after computing so that misplaced digits and unreasonable answers are detected.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Number Talk PLC Activity. Use place value to represent the number, select an efficient operation or comparison strategy, and verify the magnitude of the result.

translations.title: True or False?
translations.explanation: True or False? is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:5.NF.A.1. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators (including mixed numbers) by replacing given fractions with equivalent fractions in such a way as to produce an equivalent sum or difference of fractions with like denominators. For example, 2/3 + 5/4 = 8/12 + 15/12 = 23/12. (In general, a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/bd.) Instructional focus: Students interpret fractions as numbers and as relationships between equal parts and a whole, then use equivalent forms and operations only when their meaning is preserved. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: True or False?. The denominator tells how many equal parts make one whole; the numerator counts those parts. Equivalent fractions name the same point or quantity. For addition and subtraction, units must be the same size; for multiplication or division, interpret what is being scaled or shared.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: Add fractions with the same unit: 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. This equals 3/4 in simplest form. Example 2: Add fractions with the same unit: 2/7 + 4/7 = 6/7. This equals 6/7 in simplest form.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: both fractions count 4ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 2+1=3. Step 3: keep denominator 4. Step 4: simplify 3/4 to 3/4 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness. Step 1: both fractions count 7ths, so the unit is already common. Step 2: add the numerators: 2+4=6. Step 3: keep denominator 7. Step 4: simplify 6/7 to 6/7 and compare it with 1 for reasonableness.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: True or False?. Do not add denominators when adding fractions. Do not cancel terms across addition. Always ask whether the fraction is less than, equal to, or greater than one when estimating the reasonableness of an answer.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: True or False?. Identify the fractional unit, preserve equal-sized parts, use equivalence when needed, perform the operation, and check the size of the answer.

translations.title: Ułamki — True or False?
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Ułamki — True or False?” należy do działu „Putting It All Together” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:5.NF.A.1. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń interpretuje ułamki jako liczby oraz jako relację równych części do całości, a następnie stosuje ułamki równoważne i działania wtedy, gdy zachowane jest ich znaczenie. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Ułamki — True or False?. Mianownik mówi, na ile równych części podzielono całość, a licznik wskazuje liczbę takich części. Ułamki równoważne opisują tę samą liczbę. Przy dodawaniu i odejmowaniu części muszą mieć ten sam rozmiar; przy mnożeniu i dzieleniu trzeba interpretować skalowanie lub podział.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Dodaj ułamki o tej samej jednostce: 2/4 + 1/4 = 3/4. Po skróceniu otrzymujemy 3/4. Przykład 2: Dodaj ułamki o tej samej jednostce: 2/7 + 4/7 = 6/7. Po skróceniu otrzymujemy 6/7.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: oba ułamki opisują części 1/4, więc jednostka jest wspólna. Krok 2: dodaj liczniki: 2+1=3. Krok 3: zachowaj mianownik 4. Krok 4: skróć 3/4 do 3/4 i porównaj wynik z 1. Krok 1: oba ułamki opisują części 1/7, więc jednostka jest wspólna. Krok 2: dodaj liczniki: 2+4=6. Krok 3: zachowaj mianownik 7. Krok 4: skróć 6/7 do 6/7 i porównaj wynik z 1.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Ułamki — True or False?. Nie dodawaj mianowników podczas dodawania ułamków i nie skracaj składników przez znak dodawania. Przy szacowaniu sprawdzaj, czy ułamek jest mniejszy, równy czy większy od jedności.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Ułamki — True or False?. Rozpoznaj jednostkę ułamkową, zachowaj równe części, w razie potrzeby użyj ułamków równoważnych, wykonaj działanie i sprawdź wielkość wyniku.

translations.title: Which One Doesn’t Belong?
translations.explanation: Which One Doesn’t Belong? is an Edulytics lesson in the unit “Putting It All Together”. It is aligned exactly to CCSS:5.MD.C.3. The accepted Common Core target text for this lesson states: Recognize volume as an attribute of solid figures and understand concepts of volume measurement. a. A cube with side length 1 unit, called a “unit cube,” is said to have “one cubic unit” of volume, and can be used to measure volume. b. A solid figure which can be packed without gaps or overlaps using n unit cubes is said to have a volume of n cubic units. Instructional focus: Students connect measurable attributes with units, measurement procedures, representations of data, and calculations that answer a concrete question. The lesson title and source sequence determine the immediate context, while the official Standard text controls the academic boundary.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Lesson-specific focus: Which One Doesn’t Belong?. Choose a unit that matches the attribute, use equal-size units without gaps or overlaps, record the unit with the number, and interpret tables, line plots, clocks, money, area, volume, or angle measures according to the problem.
translations.workedExamples: Example 1: A rectangle measures 9 units by 3 units. Its area is 9 × 3 = 27 square units, while its perimeter is 2(9+3) = 24 units. Example 2: A rectangle measures 8 units by 4 units. Its area is 8 × 4 = 32 square units, while its perimeter is 2(8+4) = 24 units.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Step 1: identify the requested attribute and units. Step 2: for area, multiply length by width: 9×3=27. Step 3: for perimeter, add all side lengths: 2(9+3)=24. Step 4: attach square units to area and linear units to perimeter. Step 1: identify the requested attribute and units. Step 2: for area, multiply length by width: 8×4=32. Step 3: for perimeter, add all side lengths: 2(8+4)=24. Step 4: attach square units to area and linear units to perimeter.
translations.commonMistakes: Lesson-specific focus: Which One Doesn’t Belong?. A number without its unit can be incomplete. Do not mix incompatible units before converting them. In graphs, read the scale and labels before drawing conclusions; in geometric measurement, distinguish length, area, angle, and volume.
translations.quickSummary: Lesson-specific focus: Which One Doesn’t Belong?. Identify what is measured, choose or convert units correctly, calculate or read the representation, and state the result with its unit and meaning.

translations.title: Pomiar i dane — Which One Doesn’t Belong?
translations.explanation: Lekcja „Pomiar i dane — Which One Doesn’t Belong?” należy do działu „Putting It All Together” i jest dokładnie powiązana ze standardami CCSS:5.MD.C.3. Główny kierunek pracy: Uczeń łączy mierzalne cechy z jednostkami, sposobem wykonywania pomiaru, reprezentacją danych i obliczeniami odpowiadającymi na konkretne pytanie. Tytuł i kolejność pochodzą z zaakceptowanego źródła pedagogicznego, natomiast granice merytoryczne wyznaczają oficjalne standardy Common Core.
translations.keyConceptsAndRules: Cel tej lekcji: Pomiar i dane — Which One Doesn’t Belong?. Dobierz jednostkę do mierzonej cechy, używaj jednostek jednakowej wielkości bez luk i nakładania, zapisuj jednostkę przy wyniku i interpretuj tabele, wykresy, czas, pieniądze, pole, objętość lub kąty zgodnie z zadaniem.
translations.workedExamples: Przykład 1: Prostokąt ma wymiary 9 na 3 jednostek. Pole wynosi 9 × 3 = 27 jednostek kwadratowych, a obwód 2(9+3) = 24 jednostek. Przykład 2: Prostokąt ma wymiary 8 na 4 jednostek. Pole wynosi 8 × 4 = 32 jednostek kwadratowych, a obwód 2(8+4) = 24 jednostek.
translations.stepByStepSolutions: Krok 1: rozpoznaj mierzoną wielkość i jednostkę. Krok 2: pole: 9×3=27. Krok 3: obwód: 2(9+3)=24. Krok 4: przy polu zapisz jednostki kwadratowe, a przy obwodzie liniowe. Krok 1: rozpoznaj mierzoną wielkość i jednostkę. Krok 2: pole: 8×4=32. Krok 3: obwód: 2(8+4)=24. Krok 4: przy polu zapisz jednostki kwadratowe, a przy obwodzie liniowe.
translations.commonMistakes: Cel tej lekcji: Pomiar i dane — Which One Doesn’t Belong?. Liczba bez jednostki może być niepełną odpowiedzią. Nie łącz różnych jednostek bez przeliczenia. Na wykresie najpierw sprawdź skalę i opisy; w geometrii odróżniaj długość, pole, miarę kąta i objętość.
translations.quickSummary: Cel tej lekcji: Pomiar i dane — Which One Doesn’t Belong?. Ustal, co jest mierzone, prawidłowo dobierz lub przelicz jednostki, wykonaj obliczenie albo odczyt i podaj wynik z jednostką oraz znaczeniem.
